lessons.title: Inventory Management Tools: EOQ, Reorder Levels and ABC Analysis

children.text: Inventory is the most physical form working capital takes. You can walk through it, count it, and watch it gather dust. It is also where the largest single improvement in most Indian manufacturing businesses sits, because stock levels are usually set by habit, by a purchase manager's memory of one stockout in 2019, and by supplier minimum order quantities nobody has renegotiated.
This lesson covers the three tools that replace habit with arithmetic: how much to order, when to order, and which items deserve the attention in the first place.
How Much to Order: Economic Order Quantity

Two costs pull in opposite directions. Order in large quantities and you place fewer orders, saving on ordering cost, but you carry more stock. Order in small quantities and carrying cost falls while ordering cost rises. The
economic order quantity
is the point where the two are balanced and the total is lowest.

markDefs.definition: Economic order quantity. The order size that minimises the sum of ordering costs and carrying costs for an item.

body.caption: D is annual demand in units, S is the cost of placing one order, H is the cost of carrying one unit for a year

children.text: A Rajkot pump manufacturer buys 48,000 castings a year. Each purchase order costs about ₹1,200 to raise, follow up, inspect and account for. Each casting costs ₹450, and the
carrying cost
is estimated at 18% a year, which is ₹81 per unit.

markDefs.definition: The annual cost of holding one unit in stock: interest on the money tied up, storage, insurance, handling, obsolescence and pilferage.

body.caption: About 40 orders a year, roughly one every nine days

children.text: Today the company orders 4,000 castings at a time, twelve times a year, because that is the quantity the supplier quoted best rates on years ago. Compare the two policies.

body.caption: Current policy against the economic order quantity

stats.label: Working capital released

body.text: Notice the shape of the cost curve. It is flat near the bottom, which means you do not need to hit the exact economic order quantity. Ordering 1,000 or 1,400 instead of 1,193 costs almost nothing extra. What is expensive is being far from it, as ordering 4,000 clearly is.

body.title: Compute an economic order quantity
body.prompt: A packaging unit consumes 90,000 rolls of film a year. Placing one order costs ₹900 in procurement, inspection and accounting effort. Carrying one roll for a year costs ₹50. What is the economic order quantity, in units?
body.explanation: EOQ is the square root of (2 x 90,000 x 900) divided by 50, which is the square root of 3,240,000, or exactly 1,800 units. That means 50 orders a year, roughly one a week.

children.text: The formula assumes steady demand, a constant unit price, no quantity discounts and no constraints on storage or working capital. Real purchasing has all four.

In practice, use EOQ as a starting point and then adjust. If the supplier offers a genuine discount at a higher quantity, compare the discount against the extra carrying cost rather than accepting or rejecting it by instinct. If the item is imported with a long shipping lead time, the order size is driven by container economics rather than by the formula. If cash is tight, the working capital constraint overrides the cost optimum, and ordering small even at slightly higher total cost is the right answer.

The formula is also sensitive to the carrying cost estimate, which most companies pull out of the air. Build it properly: interest on the money tied up, warehouse rent and handling, insurance, and a real allowance for obsolescence and pilferage. In most Indian manufacturing businesses it lands somewhere between 15% and 25% a year, and the interest component alone is your cash credit rate.
When to Order: Reorder Level and Safety Stock
The order quantity answers how much. The
reorder level
answers when: the stock position at which a fresh order has to be placed so that material arrives before the shelf is empty.

markDefs.definition: Reorder level. The stock position at which a fresh order must be placed so that material arrives before stock runs out.

body.latex: \text{Reorder Level} = (\text{Average Daily Usage} \times \text{Average Lead Time}) + \text{Safety Stock}
body.caption: Cover the normal wait, then add a cushion for when things go wrong

body.latex: \text{Safety Stock} = (\text{Max Daily Usage} \times \text{Max Lead Time}) - (\text{Average Daily Usage} \times \text{Average Lead Time})
body.caption: Sized for the worst realistic combination of heavy demand and a slow supplier

children.text: For the same castings: usage averages 160 a day across 300 working days, the supplier normally takes 12 days, but in a bad month usage runs to 210 a day and the lead time stretches to 18 days.
Safety stock
works out to 1,860 units and the reorder level to 3,780 units.

markDefs.definition: Extra stock held to absorb higher than expected demand or a longer than expected lead time.

body.label: What the cushion costs
body.context: 1,860 units of safety stock at ₹450 each. That is the price of the insurance policy, and it should be a conscious purchase rather than an accident.

body.text: Safety stock is where inventory quietly doubles. Every stockout produces pressure to raise it, and nothing ever produces pressure to lower it. Review the actual variability in usage and lead time once a year, and cut the cushion where the supplier has become reliable.

body.title: Set a reorder level
body.prompt: A component is used at an average of 180 units a day. The supplier takes 9 days to deliver, and the business holds 700 units of safety stock. What is the reorder level, in units?
body.explanation: Reorder level is average daily usage times the lead time, plus safety stock: 180 units a day over 9 days is 1,620 units, plus 700 units of safety stock, giving 2,320 units. Place the fresh order when stock touches that level, not when the bin looks empty.

children.text: Which Items to Focus On: ABC, VED and FSN

A mid-sized factory can carry 1,500 stock keeping units. Nobody can manage 1,500 items with equal attention, and nobody should try. ABC analysis sorts items by annual consumption value so that the effort goes where the money is.

body.caption: ABC analysis of a ₹42 crore inventory

cells: Weekly review, tight reorder levels, supplier scheduling
Quarterly review, bulk ordering, two-bin system

children.text: The pattern is consistent across industries: a small minority of items carries most of the value. Spending an hour a week on the 120 class A items moves far more cash than spending the same hour spread across all 1,500.

columns.label: VED, for spares and critical inputs
points: Essential: production is impaired but continues
A cheap vital spare deserves safety stock even though ABC calls it class C
This is where ABC alone gives dangerous answers

columns.label: FSN, for finding dead stock
points: Non-moving: no issue for a defined period, often 12 months
Non-moving stock is cash that has already been spent and will not come back on its own
Review it every quarter and decide: use, discount, return or scrap

body.text: Run ABC and VED together. The combination tells you the real priority: a class A vital item needs both tight ordering and a safety cushion, while a class C desirable item needs nothing more than a bulk order twice a year and no further thought.

body.title: The stock that hurts most
body.textWithBlank: Items with no consumption at all for a defined period, typically twelve months, are classified as ___ moving under the FSN method, and represent cash already spent that will not return on its own.
body.explanation: Non-moving stock is the most expensive inventory a business holds, because it carries full carrying cost with no prospect of conversion. Every quarter, each non-moving item needs a decision: use it, discount it, return it or scrap it.

body.title: Which item gets the safety stock?
body.question: A factory carries a ₹120 imported sensor that is used rarely but stops the entire line when it fails, with a 10-week import lead time. Under ABC analysis it is a class C item. How should it be managed?
options: As class C: bulk order once a year, no special attention
Hold safety stock despite its low value, because VED classification makes it vital
Do not stock it at all, since it is used rarely
Reclassify it as class A so the purchase team pays attention to its cost
body.explanation: ABC ranks by consumption value and would ignore this item. VED ranks by consequence of unavailability, and a vital item with a ten-week lead time needs stock regardless of its price. The cost of holding two sensors is trivial next to a line stoppage. This is exactly why ABC should never be used alone.

body.title: Ninety days of stock and a bank that has noticed
body.scenario: You are brought into a Coimbatore textile machinery unit with ₹42 crore of inventory against ₹126 crore of annual cost of goods sold, which is about 122 days of stock. The bank has flagged it at the annual review. The works manager says every item is needed because customers expect delivery in four weeks and imported components take ten weeks. An initial count finds 1,500 stock keeping units, of which about 400 have had no issue in the last twelve months, carrying ₹5.5 crore of value.
body.prompt: Where would you start, and what would you target in the first six months?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the ₹5.5 crore that is already dead, because it needs no negotiation with anyone.

Split those 400 non-moving items into four buckets. Items usable in current products go back into the plan and come out of future purchase orders. Items returnable to suppliers go back, even at a restocking charge. Items saleable to other units in the same cluster, or in the second-hand market, get sold at whatever they fetch. The rest gets scrapped and written off. Realistically this converts perhaps ₹2.5 crore to ₹3 crore of cash and removes the carrying cost of the rest.

Next, run an ABC and VED split on the remaining items. Expect roughly 100 to 150 items to carry most of the value. Set reorder levels and order quantities for only those, using actual usage data rather than the works manager's judgement, and put class C items on a two-bin system so they stop consuming anyone's attention.

Then deal with the real constraint, which is the ten-week import lead time against a four-week delivery promise. That gap is genuine, and it is what the works manager is defending. The answer is not to cut those buffers blindly. It is to separate the imported critical items, which need a cushion sized from actual lead time variability, from everything sourced locally, where the cushion is usually habit. Also worth testing: a local second source for two or three of the highest-value imported items, which cuts the buffer permanently.

A realistic six-month target is 122 days down to about 95, which releases roughly ₹9 crore. Set it as a stock-days target by class rather than a single company-wide number, and report it monthly alongside stockout incidents, so the improvement is visible and so is its cost.

body.title: An inventory review that actually releases cash
steps: Pull twelve months of issue data by stock keeping unit and classify every item as fast, slow or non-moving.
Value the non-moving items, and decide item by item whether to use, return, sell or scrap.
Run an ABC split by annual consumption value, and confirm that management effort currently matches it.
Overlay a VED classification for spares and critical inputs, so cheap but vital items are not ignored.
Compute the real carrying cost, starting with your own cash credit rate and adding storage, insurance and obsolescence.
Set order quantities for class A items using EOQ as a starting point, adjusted for discounts, shipping and cash constraints.
Set reorder levels and safety stock from actual usage and lead time variability, not from memory of the last stockout.
Renegotiate minimum order quantities with suppliers on the items where they drive the stock level.
Track stock days by class monthly, alongside stockout incidents, so both sides of the trade-off stay visible.

body.text: Inventory is the only working capital line you can physically walk through. Walk through it once a quarter with the issue register in hand, and the items nobody can justify will find you.

points: Economic order quantity balances ordering cost against carrying cost, and is the square root of two times annual demand times ordering cost, divided by carrying cost per unit.
The total cost curve is flat near its minimum, so being approximately right is enough, while being far from it is expensive.
Carrying cost must be built honestly from interest, storage, insurance and obsolescence, and usually lands between 15% and 25% a year in Indian manufacturing.
Reorder level is average usage over the lead time plus safety stock, and safety stock should be sized from actual variability rather than from the memory of one stockout.
ABC analysis directs attention to the small number of items that carry most of the value.
VED classification catches cheap but critical items that ABC would ignore, and FSN finds non-moving stock that is already dead cash.
The fastest cash release in most factories is not better ordering, it is disposing of what has not moved in a year.
